The finite-sample convergence rate agrees, up to logarithmic factors and generator-approximation error, with the information-theoretic lower-bound rate under the corresponding regularity regimes. Since exact balancing need not provide the best fairness-accuracy trade-off in practice, we further propose Accuracy-Constrained Adaptive Synthetic Augmentation (ACASA), which learns both where and how much to augment by minimizing estimated fairness disparity subject to a constraint on predictive accuracy. We provide a finite-sample guarantee comparing the selected augmentation allocation with the population-optimal accuracy-feasible allocation. Simulation studies and real data application support the theoretical findings and demonstrate that synthetic augmentation can substantially reduce fairness disparities while achieving favorable empirical fairness-accuracy trade-offs.

papers.title: What Do Tokenizer Comparisons Measure? Disentangling Granularity, Root Assignment, and Word-Level Readout across Amharic and Hausa
papers.summary: Morphology-aware tokenizers are expected to help morphologically rich languages, and their reported gains over byte-pair encoding (BPE) are usually credited to their linguistic units. In both, real root assignment improves Amharic named-entity recognition over scrambled roots (+4.9 and +4.7 F1), and root-frequency structure explains little of this gain. The granularity effect changes sign across languages and implementations. We recommend decomposing tokenizer effects, and reporting the readout, before a gain is attributed to linguistic structure.

papers.title: Don't Match the Noise: Distribution Matching under Unknown Measurement Error with an Audit Sample
papers.summary: Real-world machine learning systems often operate on imperfect measurements: sensors are noisy, annotations are produced by non-experts, and scientific observations are often indirect. These results provide a principled foundation for robust distribution comparison, simulation-based inference, and learning in noisy real-world machine learning pipelines.

papers.title: Robbing Peter to Pay Paul: Cross-Attribute Externalities of Fairness Interventions
papers.summary: Fairness interventions often targets disparities associated with a single sensitive attribute in binary classification tasks. However, when multiple sensitive attributes are associated with a data subject, improving fairness with respect to one attribute does not necessarily improve it across all attributes: it may exacerbate disparities associated with other sensitive attributes, including those that are unavailable to the practitioner. We refer to these unintended effects as cross-attribute externalities of fairness. We study how fairness with respect to one sensitive attribute varies when an initially unfair classification or regression model is corrected with respect to another attribute. We characterize these externalities using Wasserstein barycentric disparities and develop a distributional framework that captures changes in both marginal and joint fairness measures. This highlights a limitation of conventional fairness evaluation, in which the success of an intervention is assessed mainly for the attribute it targets. In a jointly Gaussian model, we derive explicit trajectories for marginal and joint disparities and identify conditions under which an intervention eliminates disparities with respect to its target attribute while increasing disparities associated with another attribute. We also derive sharp partial-identification bounds on the resulting externalities when a sensitive attribute is unavailable and extend our results to categorical sensitive attributes. We illustrate these externalities using classification and regression real-data: in the classification experiments, interventions increase unfairness with respect to the hidden attribute in the majority of scenarios across more than half of the datasets considered; in the regression experiments on the ACSIncome dataset, correcting for race reduces sex disparities, whereas subsequently correcting for age increases them.

papers.title: Beyond Row-Level Prediction: Evaluating and Learning Composition for Reusable Table Representations
papers.summary: Tables are compositional, with content spread across a schema, cell values, rows, and columns. Large-scale operations such as retrieval, overlap estimation, deduplication, and data curation need these local signals composed into one reusable embedding vector per table. The sharpest contrast comes from two tabular foundation models, TabPFN and ConTextTab: although both are strong row-level predictors, their states, composed by mean, max, or three further parameter-free pooling rules, trail the strongest fingerprints. We therefore ask whether the gap lies in the encoder or in the compositional rule. Keeping ConTextTab frozen, we learn only the compositional rule over its cell states, using support-conditioned distribution matching (SCDM), a self-supervised loss we propose that matches the distribution of embedding similarities to the distribution of partition overlaps within and across tables. Across all fifteen head configurations, the learned rule raises the Spearman correlation between embedding similarity and partial-view overlap from 0.04 to 0.43-0.50 on synthetic data and improves triplet ranking, clustering, and retrieval, with smaller but systematic gains on real data. papers.title: A Theory of Cross-Validation Variance
papers.summary: Cross-validation estimates predictive performance by repeatedly splitting the data into training and validation sets, fitting the model on the first and evaluating it on the second. Every observation influences the estimate in two roles, through its own evaluation when it is held out and through the models it helps fit when it trains. The random splits determine its weight in each role. From this representation, we prove an exact finite-sample identity for the variance of the cross-validated estimate. For a given splitting scheme with a common training set size, the variance is a function of these weights, with constants of the model, the metric, and the population. It covers metrics averaged over observations, such as mean squared error, and over case--control pairs, such as the AUC. The identity shows which schemes to use. The variance decomposes into sampling variance, which depends only on the training size, and variance due to the random fold splitting, which arises when the weights change from one draw of the splits to the next. K-fold cross-validation, whose weights are equal across observations by design, is therefore variance optimal at first order; Monte Carlo and bootstrap cross-validation are not. The first-order variance of K-fold does not depend on K, and under reasonable conditions on the model leave-one-out has the smallest variance of any K-fold scheme. For the AUC the same holds for leave-pair-out, which evaluates every case--control pair. Finally, we show the cross-validated estimate is asymptotically normal with the identity's full variance. Together, these results provide a general theoretical foundation for inference on cross-validated performance and establish principles for selecting variance-optimal cross-validation designs.

papers.title: REAL Loss: Optimizing Real Expected Acceptance Length for Speculative Decoding

papers.title: Mechanism-Aware Ensemble Conditioning for Data-Limited Emulation of Extreme Events

A spectral energy budget shows that what aggregation removes from a band, no linear spectral filter can recover. Crowding alone says nothing about the benefit. That is decided by how much label energy the valley removes, which we measure for every graph. papers.title: Right for the Wrong Reasons? Evaluating Plausibility and Behavioral Change in Explanation-Guided Learning
papers.summary: Explanation-Guided Learning (EGL) promises models that are not only accurate but also rely on task-relevant evidence. papers.title: How VLMs Plan What's Next
papers.summary: When a vision-language model describes an image, it names one object at a time and it rarely repeats itself, yet how the model plans this order is far from obvious. We characterize the mechanism a VLM uses to decide where to look before it looks. The mechanism has four main parts. First, binding heads match the relevant text tokens against the image and resolve them into pointers to the matched image region. Second, the same binding heads bind each written answer to the region it came from, and the model turns it into a progress signal: a cursor, the position in the image up to which the list has been written. Third, a select step chooses the nearest unwritten region after the cursor, or stops. Finally, gaze heads execute the chosen pointer and return a concept of what is drawn there, which language heads and the late MLPs turn into a word in the language of the question. We validate each part of this mechanism through causal patching in Qwen3-VL models on a synthetic visual retrieval task, and test our mechanisms against alternative hypotheses. We further show that the mechanism holds across input formats, natural photographs, and languages, and that its binding, relay, and gaze heads appear at every model size from 2B to 32B. This work allows us to investigate how a VLM turns a question and an image into a sequence of answers, layer by layer and token by token. More broadly, it opens a way to study how models plan over complex multi-step tasks with long rollouts. Our project is available at https://plan.baulab.info/

papers.title: The cost of enforcing long-run coverage: a phase transition in online conformal prediction
papers.summary: Consider an online prediction setting, where at each time, we are given a new feature vector and asked to provide a prediction interval or prediction set that will likely contain the corresponding response. In practice, however, issues such as distribution drift, changepoints, or other challenges may cause violations of the i.i.d. assumption. In this adversarial setting, online conformal prediction methods can still offer guarantees on long-run empirical coverage. However, there is a trade-off between these two types of goals: enforcing tight constraints on long-run empirical coverage to protect against the adversarial setting can lead to unstable oscillations in the instantaneous training-conditional coverage in the i.i.d. setting. In this work, we seek best-of-both-worlds algorithms that aim to minimize cumulative error in instantaneous training-conditional coverage when in the i.i.d. setting, while also offering long-run empirical coverage guarantees in the adversarial setting. Specifically, consider a condition that requires long-run empirical coverage to deviate from the target level $1-α$ by at most $\mathcal{O}(T^{-β})$, for some $β\in[0,1]$. We prove that this family of conditions can be described with a phase transition. For $β\in[0,\frac{1}{2}]$, it is possible to construct algorithms satisfying such a constraint in the adversarial setting, while offering the same instantaneous coverage performance as split conformal prediction if the data is in fact i.i.d. On the other hand, for $β\in(\frac{1}{2},1]$, this type of condition comes at a cost, and does not achieve best-of-both-worlds behavior.

papers.title: Almost Controlled: The FDR of Benjamini-Hochberg on Weighted Conformal p-Values
papers.summary: Weighted conformal p-values generalize conformal inference to cases with covariate shift. With $n$ calibration points, $m$ test units and weight ratio $B$, the relative excess $\mathrm{FDR}/q-1$ is bounded by a function of $n$, $m$, $B$ and $q$ that is of order $\sqrt{Bm/(nq)}$ when $Bm/(nq)$ is small. The bound holds for every configuration with $B\le n$ and every $n$. This order can be reached when multiple non-null test units share a common threshold: in a Poisson-limit model, that configuration's excess is $c(q)\sqrt{Bm/(nq)}$ to first order as $B/n\to0$ and then $m\to\infty$. For some fixed distributions with this structure, the excess decreases only like $n^{-1/2}$ as $n$ grows. If every test unit is null, the excess is $O(B/n)$ at fixed $m$, and in certain configurations it grows linearly with $m$. papers.title: Variational Monte Carlo for Quantum Excited States via Nested Low-Rank Approximation
papers.summary: The electronic Schrödinger equation encodes a molecule's electronic structure and quantum properties, but solving it scales exponentially with the number of electrons. Solving this equation with neural-network variational Monte Carlo (VMC) has reached chemical accuracy on the ground state of small molecules; extending this success to excited states is constrained by two existing paradigms. Natural excited states VMC (NES-VMC) is penalty-free, but it combines the $K$ ansatzes into one determinant, whose local energy requires $K^2$ Laplacians per step. The reparameterized objective admits a VMC-compatible stochastic gradient estimator via MCMC sampling from the per-state Born densities, and a sequential nesting scheme recovers the lowest $K$ eigenstates in eigenvalue order. The resulting algorithm, NestedLoRA-VMC, inherits a global optimality guarantee from the LoRA principle. papers.title: Self-attention is a Dyson equation for many-body machine learning

papers.title: PAIR-CI: Calibrated Conditional Independence Testing for Causal Discovery with Incomplete Data

papers.title: Wavelet-Energy-Driven Dynamic Patching for Time Series Forecasting
papers.summary: Patch-based transformers tokenise a time series into fixed-size, uniform windows, which commits the model to a single temporal resolution even though real signals are multi-scale. That assumption has rarely been tested in isolation, because a single reported improvement usually credits three things at once. These are the use of any multi-resolution decomposition, the choice of wavelet and training the filter. A frozen wavelet beats a fixed-patch baseline on eight of the nine datasets by 1.5% to 7.8%, and on four of them it recovers all of the gain. Traffic is the one exception, where it is 1.2% worse. Second, learning the filter gives a further improvement on only some datasets. It helps on three of the nine datasets and makes Traffic 2.7% worse. Third, having variable-length patches helps, but exactly where their boundaries fall does not. A fixed-size uniform grid, even with its patch size tuned per task, is worse than our variable-length patches on 27 of 36 settings. Recomputing the boundaries from the learned filter at every step, rather than caching them once, never helps. The improvement in wavelet-based forecasting comes from the multi-resolution structure and the variable-length patches it induces, not from making the wavelet learnable. papers.title: Storage and Learning phase transitions in the Random-Features Hopfield Model

papers.title: Temporal Regularized Learning: Self-Supervised Learning Local in Space and Time
papers.summary: Self-supervised objectives such as VICReg learn representations by making related inputs similar, while variance and covariance penalties prevent collapse. These penalties are statistics over a batch of samples, so layer-local variants, too, are typically local in space but not in time. We introduce Temporal Regularized Learning (TeReL), which optimizes a VICReg-style objective one sample at a time with purely local updates: each update uses only the current activity of its own and the preceding layer and a fixed-size running state. Temporally adjacent inputs serve as positive pairs, which makes the objective a soft form of Slow Feature Analysis (SFA). Running estimates of each neuron's mean and variance, together with one lateral matrix per layer, replace the batch statistics; held fixed during differentiation, they turn the gradient into a Hebbian feedforward update and an anti-Hebbian lateral update. We show that a two-layer network trained with batch size one on an MNIST stream of class-homogeneous chunks reaches 96.48% linear-probe accuracy, above random features (95.09%) and classical SFA, and that the temporal order and each loss term contribute to this result. With both locality constraints relaxed, the same objective matches supervised backpropagation. TeReL thus shows that the collapse-preventing statistics of modern self-supervised learning can be held as running state at each neuron, which brings these objectives closer to what brains and neuromorphic hardware can implement.

papers.title: The Limits of Closed-Form Couplings for Few-Step Generation
papers.summary: Few-step generators via flow models require complicated technical solutions such as a pretrained flow model or a consistency loss. While rectified flows have gained popularity for their success in few-step sampling, they pay a cost of needing a pre-trained model and sampling a large number of couplings per dataset. Yet for a finite dataset and a Gaussian probability path, the probability-flow vector field of the empirical distribution is available in closed form, so one could use this field as the teacher and skip pretraining altogether. We demonstrate that, surprisingly, this approach is impossible for problems of practical relevance. In particular, the analytic solution of the diffusion process in high dimensions becomes almost a linear transformation. The integration returns the noise vector drawn at initialisation, plus a drift that is empirically a faint copy of the data point, almost independent of the noise. The coupling therefore differs from an independent pairing only through this drift. As a result, training a model on these couplings is almost equivalent to training the model on the independent draws of the noise and the data, which does not provide a useful teacher. We highlight that this is the direct consequence of the high-dimensionality of the data, and that for low enough dimensions or large enough datasets, analytic couplings become more efficient teachers. We quantify this effect by the fraction of endpoint energy carried by the drift, which scales as $\frac{\log N}{d}$ for a dataset of size $N$ in a $d$-dimensional space. Finally, we provide an empirical study confirming all the theoretical results presented in the paper.

papers.title: Inside the Loop: A Mechanistic Study of Looped Transformers on Permutation Traversal

papers.title: artist: A Python package for differentiable ray tracing and gradient-based optimization of solar tower power plant operation
papers.summary: Solar tower power plants provide dispatchable, renewable energy by concentrating sunlight with thousands of mirrors, called heliostats, onto a central receiver. They cannot recover unknown plant parameters from measured flux nor directly optimize plant operation. By making the optical pipeline, comprising heliostat surface representation, kinematics, blocking, and ray tracing, end to end differentiable, artist turns the digital twin from a passive forward model into an active physics-based tool for inverse modeling and data-driven optimization. The resulting gradient-based framework unifies tasks usually handled by separate solutions, such as reconstructing heliostat surfaces and kinematics from operational flux images without costly deflectometry, predicting irradiance at the receiver, and optimizing aim points to realize a desired receiver flux density distribution. It interfaces with open data sources such as the PAINT database. We describe the software architecture, physical models, and optimization framework, and demonstrate the workflow on representative tasks. By integrating modeling, prediction, and optimization into a single open, interpretable package, artist provides a principled foundation for data-driven research toward autonomous solar tower operation.

papers.title: On the Difficulty of Sequence-Level Supervised Learning for Autoregressive Language Models
papers.summary: During the supervised learning phase, autoregressive language models are typically trained by minimizing the negative log-likelihood of the training data, which decomposes as a sum of token-level cross-entropies via teacher forcing. Can we instead design sequence-level loss functions that incorporate inference-time decoding procedures, such as greedy decoding or autoregressive sampling? We show that two natural attempts lead to loss functions that are fundamentally flawed: unbounded below. We further show that these two flawed loss functions are intimately connected: using autoregressive Gumbel tricks, the sampling based loss is the expected greedy loss under Gumbel perturbations. Since the pathology stems from the dependence of the decoded sequence on the model parameters, we analyze the update direction obtained by applying a stop gradient on the sampling procedure, leading to a moment matching direction. While it is not the gradient of any loss function, we prove that it defines a valid descent direction in function space for the autoregressive negative log-likelihood. Despite these theoretical insights, the moment matching direction suffers from high variance. We conclude that teacher forcing may well be ``all you need'' for supervised learning of autoregressive models.

papers.title: What Does a Cosine of 0.8 Mean? Monotone Calibration of Embedding Similarity

On new pairs, calibrated scores agree with human ratings and the models agree with one another. One threshold selects pairs of similar quality whatever the model. papers.title: Calibrate Once, Grow the Vocabulary: Candidate-Independent Scores for Conformal Risk Control in Open-Vocabulary Segmentation

papers.title: Conic Structure of the Cross-Entropy Loss at the Final Layer and Its Absence in Rectifier Backbones

papers.title: Fast at the Frontier, Wrong at the Fallback: A Commit-Level Analysis of Threshold Decoding in Diffusion Language Models

The accuracy loss comes from committing tokens before the text to their left, and committing one token per step does not reduce it. The worst case is an early end-of-sequence token that cuts the answer short. Fallback commits are 11-35% of commits but start 61-72% of the failures that left-to-right decoding avoids. Changing only the step where such a failure starts repairs it more often than changing a similar earlier step. Committing only at the frontier recovers most of the lost accuracy on all four models. papers.title: GPromptShield: Elevating Resilience in Graph Prompt Tuning against Adversarial Attacks
papers.summary: The paradigm of ``pre-training and prompt-tuning", with its effectiveness and lightweight characteristics, has rapidly spread from the language field to the graph field. Several pioneering studies have designed specialized prompt functions for diverse downstream graph tasks based on various graph pre-training strategies. These prompts concentrate on the compatibility between the pre-training pretext and downstream graph tasks, aiming to bridge the gap between them. However, designing prompts blindly to adapt to downstream tasks based on this concept neglects crucial security issues. By conducting covert attacks on downstream graph data, we find that even when the downstream task data closely matches that of the pre-training tasks, it is still feasible to generate highly misleading prompts using simple deceptive techniques. In this paper, we shift the primary focus of graph prompts from compatibility to vulnerability issues in adversarial attack scenarios. We design a highly extensible shield defense system for the prompts, which enhances their robustness from two perspectives: Direct Handling and Indirect Amplification. When downstream graph data contains unreliable biases, the former directly combats invalid information by incorporating hybrid multi-defense prompts to the input graph's feature space, while the latter adopts a training strategy to bypass the invalid components and amplifies valid part. We provide a theoretical derivation that proves their feasibility, indicating that unbiased prompts exist under certain conditions on unreliable data. Extensive experiments across various scenarios of adversarial attacks indicate that the prompts within our defense system exhibit enhanced resilience and superiority. This paper explores a new perspective in graph prompt learning, offering a novel option for robust prompt tuning in downstream tasks.

papers.title: DNA: A Double-Helix Hierarchical Deep Interaction Network Architecture for Industrial Digital Twin
papers.summary: High-fidelity modeling is fundamental to industrial digital twin, yet a trade-off persists between the physical transparency of mechanistic models and the superior predictive power of data-driven approaches. Existing hybrid methods often fail to bridge this gap, suffering from shallow integration and rigid one-shot modeling strategies that struggle with complex industrial systems. To address these issues, we propose a \textbf{Double-Helix Hierarchical Deep Interaction Network Architecture (DNA)}. Inspired by the double-helix structure of biological \textit{DNA}, our architecture intertwines mechanistic and data-driven modeling strands through two novel interaction strategies, forming a symbiotic architecture in which the two strands mutually enhance predictive capability. Furthermore, the hierarchical structure of DNA allows it to model complex systems in a multi-stage manner through two tailored deep learning frameworks. We evaluate the proposed approach on two distinct industrial systems, where DNA achieves reductions in MAE of 3.704\% and 3.175\%, respectively, compared to the strongest baseline. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of DNA and suggest its potential to provide new insights for the development of industrial digital twins.

papers.title: Quantum Computing-Based Wasserstein Generative Adversarial Networks for Airfoil Parameterization
papers.summary: Airfoil geometry parameterization is essential in aerodynamic design optimization. Optimization search in the large space suffers from low efficiency and modest feasible region, which could further incur failures to convergence. Generative adversarial networks (GAN), aiming to learn the statistical distribution of existing data, pave a new avenue for shape generation and airfoil parameterization. GAN manages to implicitly reduce design space by generating only smooth, realistic airfoils. Meanwhile, quantum computing has been emergingly exhibiting great potential for achieving superior performance in specific types of engineering problems but has not been introduced to airfoil parameterization. To fill this gap, this work develops quantum computing-based Wasserstein GAN (Q-WGAN) and investigates the performance for airfoil parameterization. The Q-WGAN adopts parameterized quantum circuits as the generator to promote the generative performance, while the discriminator remains classical. The developed Q-WGAN is demonstrated on a dataset of optimal airfoils parameterized by free-form deformation (FFD) control points, resulting from 992 airfoil aerodynamic design optimizations. Results show that Q-WGAN achieves 92.1% mean fitting accuracy on the optimal FFD control points and 99.2% accuracy on airfoil coordinates, comparable with the classical WGAN performance of 92.28% on FFD control points and 99.26% on airfoil coordinates. Q-WGAN achieves lower Jensen-Shannon divergence, Fréchet distance, and Wasserstein distance than the classical WGAN, indicating an improved agreement with the reference airfoil distribution. Therefore, this work presents a convincing evidence that Q-WGAN makes a viable option for parameterizing airfoils and possesses a great potential for other relevant engineering applications.

papers.title: RoShift: Lazy Shift and Weight-aware Rotation for Activation Sparsity in LLM Inference
papers.summary: Activation sparsity accelerates LLM decoding by skipping unnecessary weight reads and computation. However, SiLU-based LLMs exhibit little natural sparsity, and imposing high sparsity can substantially degrade accuracy. We propose RoShift, a training-free method that transforms activations into sparsity-friendly representations. RoShift introduces lazy shift, which recenters SiLU activation distributions around zero and defers correction to the end of the FFN to obtain additional sparsity. It also reduces sparsification-induced output error through rotation that jointly accounts for activation and weight information. By fusing the corrections required for shifting and rotation, RoShift translates these gains into decoding speedup. At 50% and 60% sparsity, RoShift improves average accuracy over TEAL by 1.60 and 3.29 percentage points, respectively, across five models. It achieves up to $1.72\times$ decoding speedup over the dense model on an RTX 5090 at 50% sparsity and yields a better accuracy-speedup Pareto frontier than TEAL. Code is available at https://github.com/hulahula3247/RoShift

papers.title: Local-Order Auxiliary Losses Can Improve Autoencoder Reconstruction
papers.summary: Mean-squared error is the default objective for training autoencoders, yet compressed reconstructions often depend not only on pointwise accuracy but also on preserving local spatial order. We study whether structural auxiliary losses can improve, rather than trade off against, MSE in finite-capacity autoencoders. We introduce finite-difference sign error (FDSE), a local-order auxiliary objective that penalizes disagreements between the signs of neighboring finite differences in the target and reconstruction. FDSE is simple, architecture-agnostic, and differentiable through smooth sign surrogates. Across four tensor reconstruction tasks, we find that moderate mixtures of MSE and FDSE can substantially reduce validation MSE relative to pure MSE training. In coefficient sweeps, FDSE mixtures reduce validation MSE by 2.3$\times$--7.0$\times$ over pure MSE on these tasks, while comparisons with other auxiliary objectives show FDSE to be among the strongest structural objectives tested. The effect is not universal: pure FDSE performs poorly, and gains are largest for coherent spatial fields where local order carries information about the underlying signal. These results suggest that, in compressed-latent reconstruction, appropriately weighted local-structure supervision can guide optimization toward solutions with better pointwise accuracy, rather than merely improving perceptual or structural metrics at MSE's expense.

papers.title: GaugeRoPE: RoPE-Compatible Executable Latent Attention
papers.summary: Latent KV cache compression reduces memory footprint by mapping historical keys and values into compact representations. However, generic compressed key states require reconstruction to native dimension before applying RoPE and computing attention scores, adding sequence-scaling overhead to the decode path. We characterize when a latent KV representation can serve directly as the execution state of pretrained RoPE. For RoPE-based transformers, exact static linear execution of the rotary key path requires the latent-to-native map to preserve the pretrained RoPE action through an intertwining relation, restricting exact mixing to coordinates that share the same RoPE frequency. Guided by this characterization, we build GaugeRoPE, a training-free executable latent KV representation. It combines a RoPE-compatible carrier that preserves the rotary action with an approximate position-independent residual key--value (RKV) correction for complementary key and value information, both evaluated without per-token dense historical K/V reconstruction. On Mistral-7B, GaugeRoPE achieves $5.85\times$ KV compression while maintaining quality close to the full-cache baseline. Additional MHA results validate the construction beyond GQA. GaugeRoPE achieves up to $2.48\times$ the decode throughput of the vanilla uncompressed baseline through direct latent execution.

papers.title: Dynamic Load Model for Data Centers with Pattern-Consistent Calibration
papers.summary: The rapid growth of large-scale data centers has made accurate dynamic data center load modeling increasingly important for power system analysis. Such loads are characterized by fast workload-driven variability and protection-driven disconnection and reconnection behavior that are not captured by conventional load models. Existing approaches to data center load modeling include physics-based methods, which provide interpretable structure for grid simulation, and data-driven approaches, which capture empirical workload variability from data. However, physics-based models are typically uncalibrated to facility-level operation, while trajectory alignment in data-driven methods often leads to overfitting and unrealistic dynamic behavior. To resolve these limitations, we design the framework to leverage both physics-based structure and data-driven adaptability. We further show that trajectory-level alignment is limited for inherently stochastic data center loads. Therefore, we design the calibration to align temporal and statistical patterns using temporal contrastive learning (TCL). This calibration is performed locally at the facility, and only calibrated parameters are shared with utilities, reducing the need to share full-resolution operational time-series traces with utilities. The proposed load model is calibrated by real-world operational load data from the MIT Supercloud, ASU Sol, Blue Waters, and ASHRAE datasets. Then it is integrated into the ANDES platform and evaluated on the IEEE 39-bus, NPCC 140-bus, and WECC 179-bus systems. We simulate the collective dynamic responses of multiple heterogeneous data centers under system-level disturbances. We find that interactions among data centers can fundamentally alter post-disturbance recovery behavior, producing compound disconnection-reconnection dynamics and delayed stabilization that are not captured by uncalibrated load models.

papers.title: Parallelizable Interior-Point ADMM for Block-Structured Nonconvex Programs
papers.summary: Physics simulation is an increasingly important computational primitive for AI, and local--global/ADMM splitting exposes its parallel structure but lacks matching finite-time convergence guarantees. We close this gap with two ADMM variants, Interior-Point ADMM (IP-ADMM), for block-structured nonconvex composite programs with smooth nonlinear inequality and affine constraints. A one-sided finite-activation wall keeps each constraint split state strictly feasible while the original-space infeasibility vanishes, giving closed-form constraint updates, one proximal call per objective block, and one equality-constrained quadratic consensus solve per iteration. \rev{To our knowledge, this makes IP-ADMM the first single-loop method that updates nonconvex inequality constraints locally and in parallel with finite-time convergence guarantees.} Ordinary IP-ADMM attains a CQ-free best-iterate weak-KKT rate of $O(K^{-1/3})$ or a banded Fritz--John rate of $O(K^{-1/4})$, which converts to KKT at $O(K^{-1/4})$ under a uniform constraint qualification; these are nearby-point certificates that reduce to conventional KKT for smooth blocks. A checkpoint variant, IP-ADMM-Ckpt, improves the asymptotic KKT exponent to $O(K^{-1/3})$. We also show how the bounds scale with the objective- and constraint-block counts and the coupling norm.

papers.title: Faster Algorithms for Structured Linear and Kernel Support Vector Machines
papers.summary: Many machine learning problems are quadratic programs, including Support Vector Machines (SVMs). A general quadratic program has input size $Θ(n^2)$, and assuming the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH), no $O(n^{2-o(1)})$ time algorithm exists when the objective matrix is positive semidefinite (Backurs, Indyk, and Schmidt, NeurIPS'17). SVMs, however, are given by $n$ data points of dimension $d$, often much smaller than $n$, and have only $O(1)$ equality constraints. In this work, we design the first nearly-linear time algorithm for solving quadratic programs whenever a low-rank factorization of the quadratic objective matrix is given, the number of linear constraints is small, the coefficients of the objective and some optimal solution are bounded by $\mathrm{poly}(n)$, and some feasible point has all entries between $1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$ and $\mathrm{poly}(n)$. For linear SVM on $d$-dimensional data, our randomized algorithm runs in expected time $\widetilde O(nd^{(ω+1)/2}\log(n/ε))$ when $(d+1)^{ω-1}\le n$ and the data points have norms at most $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ and margin at least $1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$, where $ω<2.258$ is the matrix multiplication exponent. Its output satisfies the equality constraint only approximately. For Gaussian kernel SVM, when $d=O(\log n)$, the squared dataset radius is $o(\log n/\log\log n)$ and the dual variables lie in a box $[0,R]^n$ with $R\le\mathrm{poly}(n)$, our randomized algorithm runs in expected time $n^{1+o(1)}$ for any accuracy $ε\ge 1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$. We also prove that, assuming SETH, when the squared dataset radius is $Ω(\log^2 n)$, $Ω(n^{2-o(1)})$ time is required on some inputs to reach error $\exp(-Θ(\log^2 n))$ for the program without the bias term. This improves upon the prior best lower bound in both the dimension $d$ and the squared dataset radius.

papers.title: On the Applicability of $p$-adic Numbers in Computational Modules for Neural Networks
papers.summary: The applicability of $p$-adic arithmetic as an intermediate computational module in an otherwise unchanged machine-learning pipeline is investigated. A one-feature linear regression on the scikit-learn Diabetes dataset serves as the test model. The fitted coefficients are represented in $\mathbb{Q}_p$, predictions are computed in that field, and rational reconstruction is applied to the outputs. In the pyAdic experiments, rational reconstruction either returns no result or produces values that differ from the baseline predictions; changing computational precision can change both the magnitude and sign of the reconstructed value. In SageMath, forward conversions succeed, but the reconstructed predictions differ from the baseline. An alternative representation based on digit reversal fails to preserve ordinary addition because of carry propagation. Under the tested settings, none of the test predictions is reconstructed correctly. These results show that the tested conversion and reconstruction procedures do not provide a compatible intermediate module even for linear regression. Models defined directly over $p$-adic data and operations offer a direction for further investigation.

papers.title: AdaModalX: Synchronization-Free MFM Inference for Distributed Multimodal Mobile Sensing via Progressive Data Orchestration
papers.summary: Multimodal foundation models (MFMs) support generalizable inference in distributed mobile sensing applications by integrating heterogeneous data streams. However, existing MFM inference pipelines typically require complete and synchronized multimodal inputs, whereas mobile sensing streams arrive asynchronously due to network variability and heterogeneous data volumes across modalities. Waiting for all modalities increases end-to-end latency, while inference with incomplete inputs can reduce accuracy. We argue that multimodal inference should depend on the utility of available information rather than modality completeness. Based on this principle, we propose AdaModalX, a progressive multimodal inference framework that decouples inference execution from modality synchronization through runtime utility-aware orchestration. At each device, importance-aware data uploading uses a lightweight probe distilled from the edge-side MFM to allow reliable samples to exit locally while uncertain samples continue uploading. At the edge, on-demand MFM activation constructs candidates from fully received samples and, when needed, imputed features derived from partially received delayed inputs. A lightweight contribution assessor built on frozen MFM encoders estimates candidate utility and activates the MFM once the candidate meets its corresponding utility threshold. Experiments on four mobile sensing applications show that AdaModalX improves the accuracy-latency trade-off, achieving up to 26.97% accuracy improvement and up to 64.75% end-to-end latency reduction.

papers.title: VISTA: A Framework for Vision-Informed Semantic Traffic Awareness
papers.summary: The Internet of Things (IoT) is transforming intelligent transportation systems by connecting roadside cameras, edge computing units, vehicles, and traffic infrastructure into a shared sensing and decision-making ecosystem. However, transmitting raw traffic video over vehicle-to-everything (V2X) links is bandwidth-intensive, while deploying large multimodal models directly on resource-constrained vehicles is often impractical. To address these limitations, this article proposes VISTA (Vision-Informed Semantic Traffic Awareness), a multimodal vision-language edge-intelligence framework that combines predictive video representation learning with lightweight language-based reasoning to provide communication-efficient traffic situational awareness. In the proposed architecture, roadside surveillance units employ the Video Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (V-JEPA) and an attentive-pooler module to convert traffic video clips into compact future-scene embeddings. These embeddings are transmitted through V2X links to vehicle-mounted systems, where a TinyLlama small language model, enhanced with a custom visual adapter, interprets the embeddings alongside natural-language (NL) traffic queries. VISTA enables vehicles to obtain interpretable traffic information, reason about upcoming scene dynamics, and identify potential collision risks without receiving raw video streams. Experimental results in a digital-twin urban traffic environment show that VISTA achieves 97.77% accuracy and an 89% F1 score for future collision prediction while reducing the communication payload by several orders of magnitude compared with raw RGB video transmission. These results demonstrate the feasibility of embedding-based multimodal intelligence for low-latency, communication-efficient, and safety-oriented IoT-enabled transportation systems.

papers.title: Training Multi-Layer Over-Parametrized Neural Network in Subquadratic Time
papers.summary: We consider the problem of training the last layer of a multi-layer over-parametrized neural network to minimize the empirical risk induced by a loss function. In the typical setting of over-parametrization, the network width $m$ is much larger than the data dimension $d$ and the number of training samples $n$ ($m=\mathrm{poly}(n,d)$), which induces a prohibitively large weight matrix $W\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}$ per layer above the first. Naively, when the layer inputs are dense, one has to pay $O(m^2)$ time to read the weight matrix and evaluate the neural network function in both forward and backward computation. To reduce the training cost per iteration, we propose a framework that uses $O(m^2nL)$ time in the initialization phase and achieves a truly subquadratic amortized cost per iteration in terms of $m$, i.e., $m^{2-Ω(1)}$ per iteration. The speedup comes from a sparse activation, a shifted ReLU whose threshold at each layer is proportional to the norm of the layer input. With this threshold every layer is positively homogeneous, so our convergence proof needs a width only polynomial in the depth $L$, in $n$ and in the inverse smallest kernel eigenvalues. The inputs of the trained layer are fixed and sparse. In this setting, simpler algorithms without a data structure reach the same cost per iteration, and maintaining the products of the last layer with its inputs lowers it to $mn^{ω-1+o(1)}$, where $ω$ is the matrix multiplication exponent. Our result can be viewed as an idealized model of maintaining a small amount of state on top of a frozen pre-trained model to speed up fine-tuning, a core procedure to deploy large language models (LLMs). Our guarantees assume that the frozen layers are random, and for a pre-trained model only the cost per iteration of maintaining these products carries over.

papers.title: On the Convergence of Continuous-Time AdamW
papers.summary: Continuous-time AdamW provides a framework for understanding whether an optimizer widely used to train large-scale neural networks settles to an equilibrium or sustains persistent motion. We study this long-time behavior while retaining bias correction and fixed positive weight decay. Under suitable assumptions, we establish that the dynamics are well defined for all time and remain bounded when the decay is sufficiently small. Our main result connects their limiting behavior to the geometry of the objective: trajectories approach a locally invariant manifold whose dimension equals the Hessian nullity along the associated critical component. When critical points are isolated and have at most one such direction, the trajectory converges to a single equilibrium. With two degenerate directions, however, bounded persistent motion can occur even for a smooth, strictly convex objective with a unique minimum. We also quantify how close the long-time trajectory remains to the critical set as weight decay decreases, without assuming convergence to a point. These results identify objective geometry as a key to understanding when continuous-time AdamW converges and when persistent motion is possible.

papers.title: iEEG Can Help EEG: Improving Clinical Scalp EEG Analysis through Intracranial Priors
papers.summary: Scalp electroencephalography (EEG) is a cornerstone of clinical brain monitoring, making the quality of its signal fundamental to downstream tasks and models. However, that signal is heavily contaminated by non-neural interference and blurred by volume conduction. Existing methods operate almost exclusively within the scalp modality, so they inherit the contamination they would need to overcome. In practice, intracranial EEG (iEEG) observes the neural activity with far higher fidelity, yet it is invasive and therefore scarce, and the two modalities are rarely recorded as pairs at scale, share no common channel space, and offer no clean ground truth to directly supervise a mapping. Motivated by the neuronal synchronization mechanism shared by the two modalities, we propose a reprogramming approach that fits a signal-to-signal model on iEEG alone and freezes it as a cross-modal prior. We introduce ReBrain, a framework to transfer an iEEG-learned prior to scalp EEG, which re-expresses any scalp signal through that prior and can be inserted upstream of any downstream model with no pairing or fine-tuning. ReBrain consistently improves host models across recordings from multiple hospitals and across architecture families, and our analysis traces this gain to genuine neural structure carried by iEEG rather than to the architecture itself. This work provides evidence that a scarce clean modality can serve as a transferable prior for an abundant noisy one, offering a general recipe for cross-modal transfer among biosignals. Our code is available at https://github.com/Xianglong-Bao/ReBrain.

papers.title: Routing in Gradient Space: Balanced Usage Is Not Expert Specialization
papers.summary: Sparse expert models can distribute traffic evenly while still grouping incompatible training signals within the same experts. We study routing as a gradient-partitioning problem and introduce gradient-aligned routing (GAR), whose load-normalized router objective rewards grouping observations with aligned gradients. On five multi-task text-classification mixtures, we compare GAR with task-loss-only routing, gradient-combination and gradient-conflict methods, and load-balancing losses. With a fully trainable RoBERTa backbone and classification-head experts, GAR has the highest aggregate validation accuracy, 1.07 percentage points above task-loss-only routing. With frozen DeBERTa and Qwen3-1.7B backbones and low-rank adapter experts, it again ranks first, 1.10 points above task-loss-only routing, with better-balanced expert load and higher gradient-mass purity, the share of each expert's gradient-norm mass from its dominant task; the load-balancing losses flatten load further but leave this purity near its task-loss-only level. Top-1 routing, trainable full-parameter feed-forward network (FFN) experts, and a larger backbone also show positive aggregate gains. In component ablations, the objective's cross-observation alignment terms alone retain GAR's accuracy, and GAR keeps its accuracy when observations are formed without task identity; supervising the router with task labels raises task-expert association without adding accuracy. The results distinguish expert-load balance from gradient-based routing organization and show the predictive value of gradient-informed routing in multi-task text classification.

papers.title: Test-Time Speculation
papers.summary: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM inference by using a fast draft model to generate tokens and a more accurate target model to verify them. Its performance depends on the $\textit{acceptance length}$, or number of draft tokens accepted by the target. Our studies show that the acceptance length of even state-of-the-art speculators, like DFlash, EAGLE-3, and PARD, degrades with generation length, reaching values close to 1 (i.e., no speedup) within a few thousand output tokens, making speculators ineffective for long-response tasks. Acceptance lengths decline because most speculators are trained offline on short sequences, but are forced to match the target on much longer outputs at inference, well beyond their training distribution. To address this issue, we propose $\textit{Test-Time Speculation (TTS)}$, an online distillation approach that continuously adapts the speculator at test time. TTS leverages the key insight that the token verification step already invokes the target model for each draft token, providing the training signal needed to adapt the draft at no additional cost. Treating the draft as the student and the target as the teacher, TTS adjusts the draft over several speculation rounds, with each update improving the draft's accuracy as generation proceeds. Our results across ten models from the Qwen-3, Qwen-3.5, DeepSeek-R1, GPT-OSS, MiniMax, and Llama3.1 families show that TTS improves acceptance lengths over state-of-the-art speculators by up to $72\%$ and $41\%$ on average, with the benefits scaling with generation lengths.

papers.title: Integrated GPU Core for Mamba-3
papers.summary: Mamba-3, the latest Mamba state-space model (SSM), enables efficient long-context modeling, matching Mamba-2 perplexity with half the state size and increasing decoding arithmetic intensity. papers.title: Latent Feedback Is a Compute and Data Amplifier
papers.summary: When high-quality data runs out, a common practice is to train on it for several epochs, but each repeat is worth less than the last. Latent feedback, which feeds each token's top-layer state into the next token's input, is another way to spend that compute, yet it has not been tested against a vanilla Transformer that spends the same compute on more epochs. papers.title: Physics-Informed Conformal Prediction: Embedding PDE Consistency into Distribution-Free Uncertainty Quantification for Neural Operators

papers.title: Measuring Coherence in Predictive Models
papers.summary: Many sequential decision-making procedures, such as active learning, implicitly assume that a model's current predictions agree with those it expects to make after updating on new data, a property we call coherence. We also introduce action coherence, which captures only the incoherence that changes a decision. What a resulting disagreement costs, however, is determined primarily by predictive accuracy. Sequential decisions depend on how a model updates as well as on what it predicts, so coherence, like accuracy, should be checked rather than assumed.

papers.title: Forests for Differences: Beyond Parametric Difference-in-Differences
papers.summary: This paper introduces the Difference-in-Differences Bayesian Causal Forest (DiD-BCF), a novel non-parametric model addressing key challenges in DiD estimation, such as staggered adoption and heterogeneous treatment effects. DiD-BCF provides a unified framework for estimating Average (ATE), Group-Average (GATE), and Conditional Average Treatment Effects (CATE). By structuring separate regression forests for cohort-specific levels, common untreated trends and treatment effects, the model directly embeds conditional parallel trends and no-anticipation restrictions into Bayesian nonparametrics. We establish non-parametric identification and integrated treatment effect consistency of the exact treatment effect posterior distribution. Extensive simulations demonstrate DiD-BCF's superior performance over established benchmarks, particularly under non-linearity, selection biases, and effect heterogeneity. Applied to U.S. minimum wage policy, the model uncovers significant conditional treatment effect heterogeneity related to county population, insights obscured by traditional methods. DiD-BCF offers a robust and versatile tool for more nuanced causal inference in modern DiD applications.

papers.title: Radar Panoptic Transformer: Semantic-Guided Mask Queries for Dynamic Scene Understanding
papers.summary: Automotive radar provides long-range sensing and direct Doppler velocity measurements, but its sparse and non-uniformly sampled point clouds pose significant challenges for panoptic segmentation. Dynamic objects often yield only a few detections amid a dominant static background, providing limiting the geometric cues for separating object instances. We propose \emph{Radar Panoptic Transformer (RPT)}, an end-to-end point-based network that incorporates radar-adaptive feature extraction with semantic-guided mask prediction. Its backbone aggregates pose-aligned temporal context through grouped vector attention and learns per-point neighborhood radii conditioned on range, azimuth, and radar cross section (RCS). Point-wise semantic predictions initialize queries at likely foreground detections and guide masked cross-attention through query-point class agreement, producing instance masks without geometric clustering. An auxiliary RCS-consistency loss matches instance-level statistics between predicted and annotated instances. RPT achieves state-of-the-art performance on RadarScenes with $71.6\%$ mIoU and $82.2\%$ PQ. We further evaluate RPT on MAN TruckScenes, where it outperforms the evaluated baselines in a long-range, full-surround radar setting with sensing ranges up to $230\,\mathrm{m}$. RPT achieves real-time end-to-end inference at $31$\,Hz on RadarScenes, exceeding the sensor frame rate.

papers.title: Prediction-Augmented Trees for Reliable Statistical Inference
papers.summary: Machine learning (ML) is increasingly central to scientific discovery, but translating ML predictions into rigorous scientific claims still requires statistical inference on gold-standard labeled data. A setting that has emerged across the sciences provides the analyst with a small labeled sample, a much larger unlabeled sample, and a pre-trained predictor, with the goal of constructing a confidence interval for a quantity of interest, as was formalized in Angelopoulos et al. (2023). In this ML-driven scientific discovery literature, labeled data is typically the binding constraint on precision while computation is comparatively unconstrained, motivating the design question of how additional computation can extract more inferential value from a fixed labeled set, a fixed unlabeled set, and a fixed predictor. To address this question, we propose the Prediction-Augmented Residual Tree (PART) estimator. PART takes the same inputs as the original PPI estimator and replaces its single global rectifier with locally computed rectifiers obtained from an adaptive partition of the feature space. We show that PART outperforms existing methods by producing tighter confidence intervals across real-world datasets from ecology, astronomy, and census reports, among other domains. We then describe and analyze PAQ, an estimator based on numerical quadrature techniques. Under appropriate assumptions on the input data, we show that the variance of PAQ shrinks at a rate of $O(N^{-1} + n^{-4})$, showing that there are settings where the rate of $O(N^{-1}+n^{-1})$ of existing methods can be provably broken.

papers.title: UrbanROI: Causal Modeling for Regional ROI Forecasting under POI Entry
papers.summary: As urban commercial environments continue to evolve rapidly, accurately modeling the economic impact of point of interest (POI) entry is essential for supporting data-driven advertising allocation, merchant onboarding, and regional business decision-making. Existing return on investment (ROI) prediction methods mainly focus on individual ads or merchants, overlooking the interaction effects among POIs and failing to capture the causal influence of structural changes in urban commercial ecosystems. In this paper, we introduce a novel research problem -- regional ROI forecasting under POI entry, which aims to predict the future ROI trajectory of a commercial region after the introduction of a new POI by modeling temporal ROI evolution and competition-driven interactions among surrounding POIs. To address these challenges, we propose UrbanROI, an intervention-aware causal forecasting framework for region-level economic outcome prediction. UrbanROI leverages an Interaction-aware Regional Graph Module to explicitly model competitive relationships among POIs based on user request contexts, spatial proximity, and request-level commercial signals, and constructs structurally aligned treatment and control graphs to simulate factual and counterfactual regional states. Extensive experiments on large-scale real-world POI and advertising datasets demonstrate that UrbanROI consistently outperforms strong baselines in post-entry regional ROI forecasting. The results demonstrate its effectiveness in temporal economic modeling, inter-POI interaction representation, and intervention-aware forecasting, providing support for regional economic analysis and business decision-making in dynamic urban commercial systems.

papers.title: Weights & Caches: LLMs Can Program Tabular Foundation Models
papers.summary: Neural networks are typically programmed through optimization, rather than by explicitly specifying their computations. Recent work on weight-space programming suggests that large language models (LLMs) can instead reason about and manipulate neural-network weights directly. In this work, we show that LLMs can directly program statistical computations in tabular foundation models (TFMs), whose parameters enable inference across different datasets. We investigate three complementary settings using GPT-6 Astra, without gradient-based optimization. First, Astra directly programs nanoTabPFN from zero-initialized weights, achieving a mean ROC AUC of 0.849 across 20 TabArena datasets, compared to 0.876 for a pretrained baseline. Second, Astra diagnoses and repairs a signed-product regression failure in pretrained TabPFN-3.5, restoring near-perfect predictions on held-out synthetic datasets while preserving performance on TabArena-Lite, with only a 0.08% average relative increase in error. Third, it writes KV-cache-editing programs that steer TabPFN-3.5's predictions on unseen synthetic datasets, demonstrating transformations such as reversing linear trends and converting sine waves into approximate square waves, without modifying model weights. Together, our findings suggest that LLM-driven programming could complement gradient-based optimization across TFMs' development and usage, while offering a new way to investigate and intervene in their internal computations.

papers.title: Cross-Subject Priors for Maximum a Posteriori Estimation of Latent Structure Influence Models in Motor-Imagery EEG With Few Trials
papers.summary: Coupled hidden Markov models such as the latent structure influence model (LSIM) describe how the sensorimotor rhythms of the two hemispheres evolve and interact during motor imagery, but subject-specific maximum likelihood (ML) estimates are unstable when few trials are available. This paper derives a maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimator for the LSIM whose conjugate prior equals the expected statistics of $λ$ pseudo-trials from a population model fitted to other subjects. The M-step remains in closed form, expectation maximization keeps its monotone ascent, and ML ($λ=0$) and the population model ($λ\to\infty$) are limiting cases. The prior strength was selected on 35 subjects of the PhysioNet EEG Motor Movement/Imagery Dataset and applied unchanged to 70 held-out subjects and to BCI Competition IV-2a. With $λ=1$ the held-out log-likelihood exceeded that of ML in 61 of 70 subjects (Holm-adjusted $p=9.1\times10^{-8}$) and in all 70 subjects with five training trials per class. A prior learned only from the PhysioNet data improved the held-out likelihood of all nine BCI IV-2a subjects at five trials per class and reduced the error of the joint transition matrix by 61%. Decoding accuracy did not improve ($p=0.17$). Cross-subject priors therefore stabilize few-trial dynamic models of motor-imagery EEG, but they do not improve decoding, which in these data relies mainly on structure shared across subjects.

papers.title: Kernel-Guided Learning of Lifted Sparse Polynomial Models of Nonlinear Dynamical Systems
papers.summary: Polynomial models of dynamical systems enable constructive analysis via sum-of-squares programming. Yet, many physical systems involve non-polynomial nonlinearities which for certain classes of systems may be inferred from the underlying physics even when the exact dynamics are unknown. We show that fitting lifted polynomial models directly to lifted data is problematic, since the exact lifting constraints render the lifted derivatives linearly dependent. Instead, we learn the dynamics in the extended state, i.e., the state together with the known nonlinearities, and obtain the dynamics of the nonlinearities via the exact lifting relations. To avoid the combinatorially large libraries that sparse regression requires when the polynomial degrees are unknown, we propose KINDy, which selects the degree of each component by kernel ridge regression before applying sparse regression to the correspondingly reduced library. We prove that, for sufficiently small noise and regularization, provided the data satisfy a rank condition, the selected degree never underestimates the true degree. On the cart-pole system, KINDy recovers the true degrees at low noise levels and achieves speedups of up to 8.5 over sparse regression on the full library, while in almost all cases yielding models that are at least as sparse and have lower or equal test errors.

papers.title: Symmetry Fingerprinting with Geometric Learnable Invariants Transformers
papers.summary: Geometric deep learning has made available a large variety of structurally equivariant neural network architectures, meaning a particular transformation of their input causes a predictable transformation of their output. But structural equivariance is a very strong inductive bias that can limit performance if chosen poorly. In contrast, choosing an architecture with low geometric bias necessitates data augmentation to obtain correct behavior; extending the training process. We propose a novel neural network architecture that is soft equivariant; we select a set of symmetry groups and during training the network will become equivariant only to those symmetry groups that are appropriate given the training data. After training we can inspect the network to obtain a symmetry fingerprint that will tell us exactly which symmetries ended up being relevant and to what degree. We show how our architecture and the fingerprinting process work in the case of an image classification task.

papers.title: Rectifying Conformity Scores for Better Conditional Coverage
papers.summary: We present a new method for generating confidence sets within the split conformal prediction framework. Our method performs a trainable transformation of any given conformity score to improve conditional coverage while ensuring exact marginal coverage. The transformation is based on an estimate of the conditional quantile of conformity scores. The resulting method is particularly beneficial for constructing adaptive confidence sets in multi-output problems where standard conformal quantile regression approaches have limited applicability. We develop a theoretical bound that captures the influence of the accuracy of the quantile estimate on the approximate conditional validity, unlike classical bounds for conformal prediction methods that only offer marginal coverage. We experimentally show that our method is highly adaptive to the local data structure and outperforms existing methods in terms of conditional coverage, improving the reliability of statistical inference in various applications.

papers.title: Estimating Continuous Treatment Effects with Two-Stage Kernel Ridge Regression
papers.summary: We study the problem of estimating the effect function for a continuous treatment, which maps each treatment value to a population-averaged outcome. A central challenge in this setting is confounding: treatment assignment often depends on covariates, creating selection bias that makes direct regression of the response on treatment unreliable. To address this issue, we propose a two-stage kernel ridge regression method. In the first stage, we learn a model for the response as a function of both treatment and covariates; in the second stage, we use this model to construct pseudo-outcomes that correct for distribution shift, and then fit a second model to estimate the treatment effect. Although the response varies with both treatment and covariates, the induced effect function obtained by averaging over covariates is typically much simpler, and our estimator adapts to this structure. Our optimal learning bounds are achieved without estimating the conditional treatment density, thereby bypassing a major bottleneck in existing methods. Furthermore, we introduce a fully data-driven model selection procedure that achieves provable adaptivity to both the unknown degree of overlap and the spectral decay of the underlying kernel.

papers.title: QA-CMIF:Accurate and Lightweight Cross-Modal Latent Imputation and Fusion for Fault-Tolerant sEMG-Inertial Hand Gesture Recognition

papers.title: Washout-free synchronization, parameter estimation and uncertainty quantification of echo state networks
papers.summary: Echo state networks (ESNs) forecast chaotic systems for several Lyapunov times. Like all recurrent networks, ESNs require a washout before forecasting, i.e., a phase in which the full state drives the network until the reservoir state synchronizes with the system. At deployment, however, sensors measure only part of the state, with noise and at a lower sampling rate than the training data. We propose a washout-free deployment of ESNs via ensemble data assimilation. In closed loop, the ESN is a Markovian dynamical system; hence, a sequential filter can correct its reservoir state whenever data are available. The filter synchronizes an ensemble of reservoir states, drawn from the training data, with the system, and quantifies the forecast uncertainty. We extend the method to parametric ESNs, to infer physical parameters, and to parallel ESNs with localization, to forecast high-dimensional systems. We test the method on the Lorenz-63 and Lorenz-96 systems. First, the filter synchronizes the ESN with a fraction of the data of a washout. Second, the filter deploys one full-state ESN from a subset of its components, which a washout cannot do. Third, the filter estimates a forcing that is not in the training data, and the estimated forcing lengthens the forecast. Fourth, localization synchronizes a parallel ESN with eight times fewer members than the global filter. Fifth, the ensemble spread signals, without the true state, when the ESN synchronizes and when the filter fails. This work enables the deployment of ESNs from partial, sparse and noisy observations.

papers.title: Continual Instruction Tuning for LLM-based Management of Continuum Resources
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for resource management across the Cloud-Edge continuum. However, embedding LLMs directly inside latency-sensitive control loops places inference latency, execution jitter, and hallucination risks on the critical path. This study argues for a different use of LLMs: a continually instruction-tuned intent compiler that runs once per management intent or declared context change, above a fast, deterministic tactical controller that handles all low-latency runtime actions. We formulate intent compilation as a continual instruction tuning problem, because management intents arrive sequentially and accumulate while infrastructure and workload contexts drift. Unlike recent LLM-based management frameworks, our design scores the model's outputs by execution, so that catastrophic forgetting can be measured in the executed objective of the underlying controller. On a continuum simulator with a 2B backbone and parameter-efficient adapters, preliminary results show that naive sequential tuning forgets earlier intents in the executed objective, that replay of stored examples nearly prevents this forgetting, and that the tuned compact compiler performs on par with simpler translators while being more robust than a grammar parser to rephrased intents. Code and data are available at https://github.com/lilanpei/continuum-intent-compiler.

papers.title: Drift-Aware Multimodal User Representation Learning via Multi-Scale Temporal Modeling and Sparse Mixture-of-Experts
papers.summary: Understanding user preferences from noisy and temporally evolving social media behaviors is fundamentally challenging due to interest drift, where user preferences shift across time and exhibit both multi-scale temporal patterns and diverse co-existing interests. papers.title: Does Learning Order Explain Forgetting? The Lie Bracket as an Early-Warning Signal for Catastrophic Forgetting Without Old Data
papers.summary: A network trained on task A and then task B ends at different weights than one trained on B and then A. To leading order this gap is set by the Lie bracket of the two tasks' gradient fields, and Dherin (2023) conjectured that a non-vanishing bracket may be linked to catastrophic forgetting. I test this conjecture empirically. Across Split MNIST, Split Fashion-MNIST and Split CIFAR-10, the forgetting of A is almost exactly the difference in A's loss between the two training orders (Spearman rho = 0.96-1.00). I then ask whether the bracket can predict that forgetting early in training on B and without any of A's data, using only a small summary stored when A finishes: its gradient and its top 20 Hessian eigenpairs. When the old task is well learned and forgetting is slow (task-incremental), this stored bracket ranks forgetting with rho = 0.70-0.81, against 0.33-0.58 for the penalty of Elastic Weight Consolidation, and matches or exceeds re-evaluating A on its own data. When forgetting is fast (domain-incremental), the stored summary goes stale and the EWC penalty is as good or better. The bracket fails outright when the old task is only half learned; I trace this to a residual gradient on A an order of magnitude larger, which makes first-order (slope) damage matter. The bracket is therefore a useful early-warning signal for the quiet kind of forgetting, under a clear condition.

papers.title: Do Search-Augmented Recommenders Use the Latest Search Episode?
papers.summary: When a user returns to a recommendation feed after searching, does the latest search episode help rank the next item? Aggregate ranking gains leave open whether search-augmented recommenders use the latest search at prediction time or benefit from broader search state and representation learning. For the full search history, the estimated contribution depends on the control. On 66,139 shared instances across three UniSAR checkpoints, neutral masking consistently lowers mean reciprocal rank (RR). In the primary assignment, matched replacements yield mean RR 0.002770 to 0.006604 higher than neutral masking across checkpoints. The adjusted intervals for this difference lie above zero under the primary assignment and all five alternative assignments per checkpoint. Search audits should specify which inputs changed and what replaced them, and report both how often ranks move and how much the original search helps.

papers.title: Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Joint Source and Parameter Estimation in Advection-Diffusion Equations
papers.summary: Source inversion problems under sparse measurements for parabolic partial differential equations (PDEs) are particularly challenging to solve using physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), due to their severe ill-posedness and the multiple unknowns involved including the source function and the PDE parameters. Although the neural tangent kernel (NTK) of PINNs has been widely used in forward problems involving a single neural network, its extension to inverse problems involving multiple neural networks remains less explored. In this work, we propose a weighted adaptive approach based on the NTK of PINNs including multiple networks representing the solution, the unknown source, and the PDE parameters. The key idea behind our methodology is to simultaneously solve the joint recovery of these unknowns thereby using the underlying PDE as a constraint that couples multiple unknowns functional parameters, leading to more efficient use of the limited information in the measurements. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical analysis of the approximation error of PINNs in a source inverse problem governed by the advection-diffusion equation (ADE) with known velocity and diffusion coefficients. In particular, we derive an error bound for the estimated source function in terms of the PINN's training error, the noise level and the discretization error. This analysis provides theoretical insight into the factors influencing the approximation accuracy. We present numerical experiments on 2D and 3D ADE using different types of measurements data reflecting practical engineering systems. Our results demonstrate the successful performance of PINNs in solving our source inversion problem and its robustness to noise in the measurements.

papers.title: Kolmogorov-Arnold Lookup Table Demappers for Amplitude Phase-Shift Keying over Nonlinear Satellite Links

papers.title: Communication-Efficient Distributionally Robust Federated Averaging with Multi-Source Data
papers.summary: Federated learning trains a shared model from distributed client data. The deployment risk is typically specified through two approximations: each unknown local distribution is replaced by its empirical distribution, and the unknown deployment mixture across clients is replaced by empirical or prescribed training weights. However, joint treatment of both approximations remains underexplored. To address this gap, we construct a global ambiguity set formed by admissible mixtures of client-wise Wasserstein ambiguity sets, yielding a distributionally robust optimization formulation. The construction allows client-dependent ambiguity radii, preserves client-wise separability of the objective function, and yields a high-probability out-of-sample guarantee for the resulting robust problem. We then introduce a penalty-based approximation of this formulation and develop a communication-efficient algorithm called BiDRO-FedAvg, for which we establish a convergence guarantee. papers.title: The structure of variational autoencoder latent spaces and its consequences for representation and optimization
papers.summary: Variational autoencoders (VAEs) are widely used to build low-dimensional representations of scientific data, with the expectation that regularization yields smooth coordinates for interpolation, generation and optimization. However, applications in microscopy reveal domains, narrow transitions and rare-state islands in VAE latent spaces that smoothness alone does not explain. We show that, for prototype data with squared-error reconstruction and an optimal decoder, the latent-space objective has a direct correspondence with the Flory-Huggins theory of a regular solution, and use it to analyze how the objective, posterior distributions and latent dimensionality organize the representation. Data families occupy domains separated by finite-width walls that broaden with increasing regularization until class separation is lost through posterior collapse. Class centroids behave like particles in a harmonic trap: the prior confines them, and structural dissimilarity sets a soft repulsion that determines which classes become neighbors and how far apart they sit, with separations growing only logarithmically with dissimilarity. Rare states can remain unresolved, form small islands, accumulate within walls or develop intervening domains, depending on their frequency and similarity to common states. The posterior covariance can align domains with the latent axes, but axis alignment does not imply separation of physical factors. Rotations can produce rings and encoder cuts that reflect data symmetry, while insufficient dimensionality can lead to suppression, mixing or folding of additional factors. Comparisons with flow models, deep kernel learning (DKL) and hybrid VAE-DKL models show how these structures change when reconstruction and prediction play different roles. We discuss implications for interpreting data, discovering rare states, generating intermediate states and optimizing properties.

papers.title: Structural interpretability in SVMs with truncated orthogonal polynomial kernels
papers.summary: Support vector machines (SVMs) can yield classifiers with similar predictive performance but different internal structures, particularly in the contributions of individual explanatory variables and their interactions. papers.title: CoSyDelay: Cognitive Symbolic Regression for Traffic Delay Estimation

papers.title: Does synthetic pre-training pay off on a microcontroller? Accuracy, latency and energy across two MCUs
papers.summary: Rendered images are cheap to label, but a microcontroller classifier must survive 8-bit integer (INT8) quantisation and compute correctly on the chip. On the RP2040 the same model took 1.80 s and 27.3 mJ above idle, about twelve times slower, and the largest 96 px model exceeded the board's flash-capacity limit. Neither the RP2040 nor the host interpreter used for scoring reproduced the reference arithmetic. A synthetic stage is worth adding only when real data are scarce, and on-device INT8 outputs should be checked against reference kernels, not inferred from host scores.

papers.title: StableRCA: Mechanism-Level Root Cause Analysis without Global Graph Discovery
papers.summary: Root-cause analysis (RCA) seeks to identify the true causal variables that are responsible for a system's abnormal behaviors. A central challenge in this task is to distinguish changes where the anomaly occurs from downstream propagated abnormal effects, particularly when the underlying causal structure is unknown.
